taskTitle: Twelve HTTP status codes, by the book

checks.detail: 3 proposers ran in parallel, one per lens
4 phases had the tools designed for them

finalText:
The current HTTP Semantics specification is RFC 9110, and every value below comes from https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html (as read by the proposals; I couldn't open the page myself).

**How cacheability was decided:** The status-code overview (§15.1) lists the codes "defined as heuristically cacheable (e.g., 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414, and 501 in this specification)". It adds that "all other status codes are not heuristically cacheable" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). Each code's own section agrees with that list:
- **Cacheable (true):** 203, 206, 308, 405, 410, 414 and 501. Each of these sections says "A NNN response is heuristically cacheable".
- **One difference for 206:** its section only says "unless otherwise indicated by explicit cache controls". It doesn't also mention the method definition, as the others do.
- **Not cacheable (false):** 303, 307, 413, 421 and 422. Their sections don't say this, and they aren't on the §15.1 list.

**Two current reason phrases worth checking:** RFC 9110 calls 413 "Content Too Large" (§15.5.14) and 422 "Unprocessable Content" (§15.5.21).

**About the quotes:** Each one comes from the code's own numbered section. The page wraps its text across lines, so the lines are joined with single spaces and nothing else is changed.
